sampleNote: Simplified from current source · setup and helpers omitted
title: Motion quality: retargeted clips & stride matching
statusNote: measured in the game on 23 September 2026
steps: Before: clips made by script in Blender (arms in rad/s², foot slide in % of distance)
After: the same bodies with motion-capture clips
definition: Retargeting copies an animation clip from one skeleton to another by matching bones by role (hips, upper arm, knee) instead of by name. Stride matching sets a clip’s playback speed (timeScale) so the feet cover the same ground as the body. Jitter is how sharply joint rotations change speed from frame to frame; foot slide is how far a planted foot moves.
impact: The Momiji cast kept the same VRM bodies. Swapping the home-made clips for the Quaternius Universal Animation Library (CC0, motion-capture quality) and fixing the pose reset made the user say the characters looked “much better and pretty”.
present: The VRM cast plays 17 clips retargeted offline into one 350 KB file, cast-clips.vrma, by asset-src/characters/vrm-cast/retarget.mjs. characters/humanoid-bones.js maps VRM, Blender, Mixamo, Quaternius, Rigify and MakeHuman joints to one set of names. Walk clips play at the body’s speed divided by the clip’s own foot speed, clamped to 0.3–1.6.
next: Add a turn-on-the-spot clip for the VRM cast; today they turn in the idle pose and a foot left behind is released and planted again. The Quaternius walk (0.92 m/s for Riko) is slower than the residents’ 1.05–1.29 m/s, so walks play up to 1.6 times faster than recorded.
accept: On the same scene before and after: idle arm jitter under 5 rad/s², walk foot slide under 5% of the distance walked, and a contact sheet of every clip with no T-pose.
tradeoff: Motion-capture clips come from another skeleton, so each needs a rest-pose check and a measured foot speed. The outside packs stay out of git; only the retargeted output is committed.
observation: Twelve frames from the retargeted Quaternius clips on Riko, Mr. Sato and Mr. Ishida. The bodies are the same VRM models as before.
exercise: Try next: take one walk clip, measure its foot speed from root motion, and play it at three body speeds. Watch a planted heel against a mark on the ground at each speed.

title: Skinned poses: never reset to rest every frame
statusNote: schematic of the bug and the fix
steps: Every bone goes back to the rest pose (a T-pose for VRM) before the clips run
three.js does not rewrite a bone whose blended value did not change
Put back the pose the clips made last frame, then add the layers
definition: A skinned mesh bends with a skeleton. The rest pose is the skeleton’s neutral pose; for VRM models it is a T-pose, arms straight out. An animation mixer blends clips and writes bone rotations, but three.js skips writing a bone when its blended value has not changed.
impact: The rig reset every bone to rest each frame so its extra layers would not pile up. Bones a clip held still were never written again, so they stayed at rest: arms snapped into a T-pose after a cross-fade settled, and Mr. Ishida stood at his bench instead of sitting. The user said they looked “like they got some disease”.
present: world/character-rig.js keeps a copy of the pose the clips made last frame. resetPose() puts it back before the mixer runs, and apply() captures the new clip pose before adding look-at, hands and feet. tests/hero-pose.test.js checks that both arms hang within 50° of straight down in every standing clip and that seated Mr. Ishida’s hips sit just above the 0.61 m bench.
next: Run the same pose test for every new cast member and clip, including clips added by agents. A render check that flags an arm more than 60° from down in a portrait would catch the bug in video too.
accept: The pose test passes for all clips; a contact sheet of the episode shows no T-pose; a seated person’s hips are no more than 0.15 m above the seat.
tradeoff: Keeping the last clip pose costs one rotation and one position copy per bone per frame. Resetting only the bones the layers touch is cheaper, but easy to break when a new layer is added.
observation: Before and after the pose fix, from the same camera. The left column is the old build and the right column the fixed one.
exercise: Try next: play a clip that holds one arm still, let the cross-fade settle for 2 s, then log that arm’s rotation with and without a rest reset before the mixer.

title: Procedural layers on top of clips
statusNote: measured in the game on 23 September 2026
steps: The clip alone, in a fresh session (jitter in rad/s²)
Look-at, hands and feet added: within 10% of the clip, or lower
definition: A procedural layer is code that changes a pose after the clip, such as turning the head toward a speaker (look-at) or bending a leg so the foot stays on the ground (inverse kinematics, IK). Each layer should own a few bones and blend in by a weight from 0 to 1.
impact: When a layer writes bones the clip is also animating, the two fight and the joint shakes. Maple Line gives each layer its own bones and its own moments, then measures each one on and off.
present: Look-at owns only the neck and head, split 40% neck and 60% head, with critically damped springs and a 0.05 rad dead zone so a speaker’s head bob does not shake the listener. Foot IK pins only the stance foot while walking, easing in over 0.12 s and out over 0.2 s. Arm IK stays off while Riko walks with walk-carry, because that clip already places her hands.
next: Turn the measurement into a check: a short headless run that reports jitter per bone group with each layer on and off, and fails when a layer adds more than 10%.
accept: Every bone group stays within 10% of its layers-off jitter, or goes down. The one known exception is Riko’s hands (0.8 to 1.7 rad/s² walking) from the radio grip, still under 2 rad/s².
tradeoff: A fair comparison needs one fresh session per condition and the development switch setDebug({ layers }), so both runs see the same events. Each layer adds a little work per character per frame.
observation: Frames from the retargeted clips with the layers on. Hands, head and feet are placed by the clip first and adjusted by the layers second.
exercise: Try next: add a look-at layer that owns only the head, then switch it on and off while a clip plays. Compare the neck’s jitter in both runs before letting the layer own more bones.

title: Character topology, retopology & base meshes
steps: A primitive tube has rings of edges only at its ends, none where the elbow bends
Bent 90°, the tube pinches at the elbow like a pipe
Retopology adds edge loops around the elbow
Bent 90°, the looped arm keeps its volume
Loops around the eyes and mouth let the face blink and smile
definition: Topology is how a mesh’s vertices and edges connect. Edge loops are rings of edges that follow a shape, like the rings around an elbow. Retopology rebuilds a rough or detailed surface as a lighter mesh with loops where it bends. Primitives (boxes, cylinders) and skin-modifier tubes have no loops at the joints, so they bend like pipes.
impact: The earlier Blender-built cast was made from primitives and skin-modifier tubes and bent like pipes at elbows and knees. The VRM cast has joint loops and facial shape keys, so it bends at the joints and can blink and smile.
present: The Momiji cast uses VRM models with MToon toon shading; the Blender-built GLBs still load with ?cast=blender. A character studio and a concept-built Riko are being built; neither is in the game yet.
next: Take the shortcut indie artists use: start from a good base mesh and customise it. Sources: Quaternius (CC0), Fab’s free Personal licence (individuals under $100k revenue) and Booth.pm (terms differ per model). Read each licence on the download day and record it in asset-src/THIRD_PARTY.md.
accept: A 90° bend at elbow and knee keeps the limb’s volume; the face has blink, smile and the main mouth shapes; the licence allows use in a public repository, or the source files stay outside git.
tradeoff: Two licence traps: the free Quaternius Universal Base Characters “Standard” pack contains only muscular superhero bodies, and Fab’s Standard licence forbids redistributing source files. The maple-line GitHub repository is public, so licensed sources stay out of git.
observation: Each Momiji cast member twice: the VRM model, then the earlier Blender-built model made from primitives and tubes.
exercise: Try next: bend one arm of a box-built figure and one arm of a base mesh with elbow loops to 90°. Compare the inside of the elbow from the side.

title: Concept turnarounds & story key frames
steps: One paragraph: age, clothes, props, face and body shape
Front, side and back in one A-pose, at one scale, on a plain background
A few frames that tell the plot with no words
The sheet sits behind an ortho modelling view so heights and joints line up; later it is projected as a paint guide
definition: A turnaround sheet draws one character from the front, side and back in the same pose and scale. An A-pose has the arms angled down, which rigs better than arms straight out. Key frames are single pictures of the main story moments. Orthographic (ortho) views have no perspective, so they line up with a 3D modelling view.
impact: Concept sheets fixed how Riko, Mr. Sato and the others look before any modelling. A few story key frames told the whole plot with no words, which showed gaps in the script early.
present: Sheets were generated with openai/gpt-image-2.5-flare through the AI Gateway at 1536 × 1024, for about $0.04 and about 25 s each. They are AI-generated concept art kept outside the repository: references, not game assets.
next: Split each sheet into front, side and back images and use them as ortho references and as a projection source. The concept-built Riko is being modelled from these sheets; it is not in the game yet.
accept: Front and side views agree on height, head size and joint positions; someone who has not read the script can retell the plot from the key frames.
tradeoff: Generated views can disagree (a hair clip that changes side, a sleeve that changes length). Compare the three views before modelling, and label generated art as generated.
file: Concept request t.req.json (kept outside the repository)
observation: AI-generated concept art, used as a modelling and story reference.
exercise: Try next: write a one-paragraph brief for a side character, make a turnaround, and mark every place where the front and side views disagree.

title: Occlusion-aware shot framing
statusNote: schematic of the current director camera
steps: Rays from the camera to the eyes and chest hit a wall
Try angles 15–90° round, then higher, lower, closer or further
Keep the first fully clear view on the same side of the 180° line
definition: Occlusion means something stands between the camera and what it should show. A sightline test casts rays from the camera to points that must be visible. The 180° rule keeps the camera on one side of the line between two speakers, so they do not swap sides of the screen between cuts.
impact: Dialogue shots stared at a wall because Mr. Ishida’s bench stood 0.6 m inside the station building. The bench was moved, and the director now checks what the camera can see before it holds a portrait.
present: camera/shot-framing.js checks the eyes and chest, tries candidateViews() in cost order, keeps the 180° rule unless nothing on its side is clear, and never picks the back of the speaker’s head. A held portrait is re-checked 4 times a second; after two blocked checks a clearly better angle may replace it, eased over 0.9 s, then held for 1.5 s. It aims at the VRM head bone. 11 of 11 Episode 1 lines show the speaker’s face.
next: Extend the full blocker list (people and props) to shot types other than portraits; today they check scenery only.
accept: Render one frame per spoken line and count the lines where the speaker’s face is visible. Read every camera: entry in the episode log.
tradeoff: Each check casts a few rays against a filtered blocker list, 4 times a second, only while a portrait holds. Glass, wires, leaves and weather never block, so a face behind a window counts as visible.
observation: One frame per spoken line of Episode 1, after the framing fix.
exercise: Try next: put a wall between a camera and a character, cast rays to the eyes and chest, and move the camera 15° at a time until both rays are clear.

title: Story structure for short videos
steps: One character wants one thing, shown in one shot
What they lose if they fail
A clock or timetable the viewer can see
What stands in the way
A person decides to help, or not
The result, shown instead of said
definition: A story beat is one change in the situation. Stakes are what a character loses if they fail. A visible clock is a deadline the viewer can see, such as a station clock or a bus about to leave. A payoff shows the result of a choice on screen instead of reporting it in dialogue.
impact: Many people watch short videos muted. The first script of The 17:42 did not work that way: its conflict was arithmetic in dialogue, nothing was at stake, the payoff was never shown, six characters shared the episode, and the bus and the clock never appeared on screen.
present: Episode 1 of The 17:42 plays in the game and renders to video with the first script. A rewrite built on this checklist is being written; it is not in the game yet.
next: Draw the beats as key frames before writing lines, keep to 3–4 characters, and put the clock and the bus in shots. Keep “how it’s made” credits out of the story video; they belong in the blog or the post that shares it.
accept: Mute the video and show it to someone who has not read the script. They can say who wants what, what stops them, who chooses and what happened.
tradeoff: Showing the clock and the payoff needs extra shots, places and props, which cost modelling and render time. Fewer characters means some of the cast get no lines.

observation: The first script’s opening lines, rendered one frame per line.

title: Deterministic video rendering
statusNote: schematic of the current render path
steps: With ?render=1 the script advances one clock by exactly 1/30 s per frame; live play has uneven gaps
Train, people, weather, camera, captions and fades all read that clock
Chrome DevTools captures each frame as a page screenshot, captions included
ffmpeg writes an H.264 yuv420p MP4 with +faststart, which plays in WhatsApp and iMessage
Voice clips are placed by line id (scene/beat/line) from the audio manifest
definition: Deterministic rendering means the same input always gives the same frames. In render mode one controllable clock drives everything, random numbers come from a fixed seed, and adaptive resolution is off. H.264 is the video codec phones play everywhere; yuv420p is its usual colour format; +faststart puts the file’s index first so playback starts before the download ends.
impact: A screen recording stutters whenever the machine is slow. Stepping a fixed clock gives a smooth 30 fps video however long each frame takes. WebM from the browser’s MediaRecorder does not play on iPhones, so the output is MP4.
present: ?render=1 exposes window.__mapleRender with ready(), play(), step(), timeline() and framing(). scripts/render-episode.mjs steps frames, captures each with Page.captureScreenshot, pipes the JPEGs to ffmpeg and mixes an audio manifest placed by line id (scene/beat/line, counted from 1). Episode 1: 88 s, 2631 frames at 30 fps, 114 s to render at 16:9 and 156 s at 9:16 on an Apple M4 Pro, about 20 MB.
next: Record the game’s own sound (train, ambience, crossing bells) into renders; today only manifest clips are mixed in.
accept: Two renders of one episode give the same frame count and timeline; the file plays in WhatsApp and iMessage on an iPhone; each caption appears on the frame where the timeline says its line starts.
tradeoff: A screenshot per frame holds the loop to about 15–18 frames per second. Capturing captions as page screenshots keeps them identical to the game, at the cost of that screenshot.
observation: Output of the render script for Episode 1.
exercise: Try next: render the same 5 seconds twice with a seeded random generator and compare the frames. Then remove the seed and compare again.

title: Multilingual voice & translation
statusNote: schematic of the current voice path
steps: Each line is written in English with its cast member
Use the episode’s hand-written translation when it has one
Otherwise machine translation, with the speaker’s gender; names stay as they are
bulbul speech; clips and translations cached on disk
The runner waits for the clip to end before the next line
definition: Text-to-speech (TTS) turns a written line into audio. Machine translation turns the line into another language automatically. A voice cache stores generated clips on disk so the same line never costs twice.
impact: Episodes can play and render with voices and subtitles in 11 languages. Costs stay small: about ₹1 per episode in English and about ₹3 in Telugu.
present: The director’s narration engine calls Sarvam bulbul:v3 for speech and sarvam-translate:v1 for subtitles, caching both under .cache/narration/. SARVAM_VOICE_MODEL selects the model; bulbul:v4-flash (224 speakers tagged by style) is allowed but beta-gated for this account, and an unknown value keeps bulbul:v3. Hand-written translations in the episode win over machine ones. drama/episode-voice.js holds each line until its clip ends.
next: Add hand-written Telugu for every line of Episode 1, and have a native speaker review each language before a voiced video is shared.
accept: A native speaker reads the subtitles and hears no wrong times, nouns or pronouns; the render timeline shows no line cut off by the next one.
tradeoff: Machine translation made three kinds of mistake in this session: a clock time read as “inches”, “front car” as “motor car”, and he and she swapped. Hand translation fixes them but costs a person’s time per language.
observation: Rendered lines with their subtitles.
exercise: Try next: machine-translate three lines containing a time, a vehicle part and a pronoun, then compare them with a hand translation. Note each change in meaning.

title: Shared links as untrusted input
steps: Refuse a #ep= payload over 12,000 characters or with odd characters, before decoding
Stop decompressing past 64 KB, so a small link cannot grow into a huge document
Require valid UTF-8 and valid JSON
The saved-episode validator refuses unknown cue types and __proto__ keys
Dialogue is set with textContent, so markup stays plain text
definition: Untrusted input is data the game did not make itself, such as a link someone else built. A decompression bomb is a small compressed payload that expands into a very large one. Prototype pollution uses a __proto__ key in JSON to change how every object behaves. textContent sets text without reading it as HTML.
impact: Anyone can make a link that opens the game on an episode, so every link is checked: size first, decompression capped, then the same validator as saved episodes. The tests include a link under 12,000 characters that expands to 4 MB.
present: Links: ?episode= (a built-in id), ?scene= (place, offset, time, weather and camera from fixed lists), #ep= (an episode as raw deflate plus base64url) and ?watch= (a short id for an episode kept in the Signal site store). share/episode-codec.js decodes; tests/share-links.test.js covers damaged, oversized and polluted payloads.
next: Test the ?watch= write path against the live Signal gateway; the unit tests use a stand-in for signal.db.
accept: Oversized, damaged, non-UTF-8, unknown-cue and __proto__ payloads each fail with a short notice, and the ride then starts normally.
tradeoff: Privacy: the Signal store records the sharer’s email (updatedBy), and anyone with site access can list the collection; say so before someone shares. #ep= links store nothing, but they are long.

spots.label: A place a link can open

observation: The station, one of the places a ?scene= link can open.
exercise: Try next: compress 4 MB of spaces into a link, then decode it with and without a byte cap. Watch memory use in both runs.

title: Parallel agents, worktrees & integration
steps: One git worktree, one branch and one dev port per agent
One owner for each area of files
Numeric acceptance criteria and the evidence to return
Merge into one integration branch early and often
Conflicts in main.js, the episode runner and docs: keep both behaviours
Read contact sheets, before/after captures and jitter numbers before merging
definition: A git worktree is a second checkout of the same repository in its own folder, so two agents can edit different branches at once. An integration branch collects everyone’s work. A hub file is one that many features touch, such as main.js.
impact: The 23 September session ran many agents at once on characters, camera framing, video, voice, sharing, water and storms, each merging into one integration branch.
present: Agents work in .claude/worktrees/<name> on their own branches. The dev server uses a strict port (4173), so it fails instead of silently opening another game, and each agent starts its own port. Render servers turn off hot reload so an edit elsewhere cannot reload a page mid-capture.
next: Before removing an old worktree, run git status inside it: git branch --no-merged lists unmerged commits but cannot see uncommitted work. Message a running agent when scope changes instead of starting a second agent on the same files.
accept: Every agent returns its numbers and evidence (jitter per bone group, a contact sheet, before/after captures), and the integration branch passes pnpm check after each merge.
tradeoff: More agents means more merges in the hub files. Agents must never touch the person’s everyday browser session; use a separate browser profile or headless runs.
observation: Evidence returned by agents in this session.
exercise: Try next: make two worktrees, change different lines of the same function in each, merge both into one branch, and resolve the conflict by keeping both behaviours.

title: Concept-to-VRM character pipeline & rigging
steps: Cut the character out of the front, side and back views; each view is scaled from head top to sole
Fill each horizontal slice with a rounded shape inside the front and side outlines
Project the painted views onto one texture, weighted by how directly each view faces the surface
Lay eyes, brows and mouth on the head as decals, with one shape key per VRM expression
Place the humanoid bones on measured landmarks: elbows at 47% of the arm, hips at 0.545 of the height

definition: Rigging gives a mesh a skeleton and says how much each bone moves each vertex (its skin weights). A VRM file is a glTF model with a standard humanoid skeleton, face expressions and spring bones, so any clip retargeted to that skeleton plays on it.
impact: Meera and Ammamma were built this way from generated concept views. Meera is about 13,600 triangles in a 684 KB VRM with a 2048 px atlas; Ammamma is about 12,600 triangles, 1.45 m tall with a 6° stoop. Both play the same 18 clips as the rest of the cast.
present: asset-src/characters/concept-cast/build.py runs matte, shape, parts, bake, face and rig in Blender headless (about three minutes), then vrm-cast/make-vrm.mjs writes the VRM. A per-character JSON file carries what the pixels cannot: height, face landmarks, masks, hair, jewellery, stoop and stance. vrm-cast/retint.mjs changes material colours in a built VRM without a rebuild.
next: Build Arjun from his own concept views (he still uses the adult commuter model), and give Ammamma loose strands at the temples so her hair stops reading as a cap.
accept: In the Character Studio, the front and side views line up with the painted views under the concept overlay; every clip in the library plays with no stretched sleeves or skirt; the build report stays near the 14,000-triangle budget.
tradeoff: The body is decimated triangles, not quads (QuadriFlow shrank thin limbs by about 10%), hands are mittens with finger bones inside, and the side profile is flat. That holds at game distance and shows in close-ups.

for side, sx in (("left", 1), ("right", -1)):
    mine = sx * x > 0
    # The torso and the far side never move with this side's arm.
    W[np.ix_(in_torso & ~shoulder_zone, arm_cols[side])] = 0
    W[np.ix_(~mine, arm_cols[side])] = 0
    W[np.ix_(~mine, leg_cols[side])] = 0

sourceCode:
def clean_body(obj, joints, m, names, W):
    """Region rules on top of the heat weights."""
    co = np.array([v.co[:] for v in obj.data.vertices])
    x, y, z = co[:, 0], co[:, 1], co[:, 2]
    idx = {n: i for i, n in enumerate(names)}

    def cols(pred):
        return [i for n, i in idx.items() if pred(n)]

    arm_cols = {s: cols(lambda n, s=s: n.startswith(s) and any(k in n for k in ARM_BONES)) for s in ("left", "right")}
    leg_cols = {s: cols(lambda n, s=s: n.startswith(s) and any(k in n for k in LEG_BONES)) for s in ("left", "right")}
    torso_cols = cols(lambda n: n in ("hips", "spine", "chest", "upperChest"))
    head_cols = cols(lambda n: n in ("neck", "head"))
    lim = np.array([m["torso_x_limit"](zz) if zz < m["z_shoulder"] - 0.035 else m["torso_half_armpit"] for zz in z])
    in_torso = (np.abs(x) < lim + 0.004) & (z > m["z_hem"])
    shoulder_zone = z > m["z_shoulder"] - 0.06
    for s, sx in (("left", 1), ("right", -1)):
        mine = sx * x > 0
        # Torso and far side never move with this side's arm (the shoulder blends).
        W[np.ix_(in_torso & ~shoulder_zone, arm_cols[s])] = 0
        W[np.ix_(~mine, arm_cols[s])] = 0
        W[np.ix_(~mine, leg_cols[s])] = 0
        # The sleeve beyond the gap follows only its arm (and the shoulder at the top).
        sleeve = mine & ~in_torso & (z > m["z_hem"] + 0.02)
        W[np.ix_(sleeve & ~shoulder_zone, torso_cols + head_cols)] = 0
        W[np.ix_(sleeve, leg_cols["left"] + leg_cols["right"])] = 0
    legs = z < m["z_hem"] - 0.01

title: A character studio for clips, layers and joints
statusNote: schematic of the Character Studio panels
steps: Load one character with the game’s own loader and show it from perspective, top, front and side
Pick a clip, scrub or step frames, and trim a range

definition: A character studio is a separate page that loads one character with the game’s own code, shows it from several cameras and gives a switch or a number for each part of its motion.
impact: Idle arms on Meera’s model jittered at 751 rad/s² and nobody could say why in the game. With each motion layer switchable in the studio, the layer fighting the clip was found in minutes; after the fix the figure is about 3.
present: character-studio.html?character=vrm/riko&clip=idle&t=1.2 opens a paused frame. It lists 11 characters and 18 clips from cast-clips.vrma. Panels: joints, motion layers, ghosts, grounding, face, concept overlay, clip editing, prop sockets and retarget preview. The page exposes its controls on window, so an agent can call measureJitter and read the result.
next: A Performance tab that plays a voiced line with its emotion, gesture and mouth curve together, so the face can be checked against the words.
accept: A number in the studio matches the same measurement in the game (same modules, not copies), and any state can be reopened from a URL.
tradeoff: It is a second app to keep working. Import the game’s modules instead of copying them, or the studio will show a character the game no longer draws.
observation: The Character Studio with Meera’s model on the idle clip at frame 36.
exercise: Try next: add one switch to your own character viewer that turns a single motion layer off, and measure what it adds.

title: Seated contact: hip height, seat reservations
steps: The cushion top is 0.5 m above the car floor; note where its front edge is
Hips at 0.62 m, not 0.50 m, so the thighs lie on the cushion
Seat point at x −1.02 m; at −1.17 m the shins go into the bench front

definition: A seated character is placed by the hips. If the hips rest at or below the cushion top, the thighs pass into the seat; if the seat point is too far back, the shins pass into the bench front.
impact: Viewers reported Meera sinking into the train seat three times. Raising the hips from 0.50 to 0.62 m fixed the thighs; moving the seat back to x = −1.17 m put her shins into the bench, so it stays at −1.02 m. Crowd riders also sat in the cast’s seats until seats could be reserved.
present: drama-stage.js marks front-car-seat as seated; main.js seats those marks at CAR_SEAT_HEIGHT (0.62 m) and renews trainModel.reserveSeat each frame. interior.js hides riders within RESERVE_RADIUS (1.2 m) of a renewed seat; a reservation lapses 0.5 s after the scene stops renewing it.
next: Read the cushion height from the car model instead of a constant, and add a thigh and skirt check against the seat in the studio’s Grounding panel.
accept: From a low side view in every seated shot of Episodes 1 and 2: no thigh below the cushion top, no shin inside the bench and no second rider in the same seat.
tradeoff: A constant is exact for this train and wrong for any other car. Keep it next to the car model and test it when the car changes.
observation: Two seated shots from Episode 2 after the fix.
exercise: Try next: seat a character on a bench, then look from knee height at the side. Raise the hips until no thigh is below the cushion, and note the value.

title: Audio-driven lip sync for VRM faces
steps: Start from the spoken WAV for the line, pauses included (Meera’s line has one of 0.45–0.9 s)
Measure loudness (RMS) 60 times a second, levelled per speaker; below 0.05 the mouth stays shut
Pick a vowel class from how bright the sound is (its spectral centroid)
Smooth: 30 ms to open, 80 ms to close; a new vowel must hold 50 ms before the mouth changes
Drive the VRM aa, ih, ou, ee and oh expressions
definition: Lip sync moves a character’s mouth from the sound of their own line. Loudness sets how far the mouth opens; how bright the sound is picks one of five vowel shapes.
impact: Mouths used to move on a fixed syllable rhythm, so they kept moving through pauses. Worse, most mouths could not be seen: the mouth colour was close to the new brown skin. Mouths were darkened with retint.mjs, and they now open on loud syllables and shut in pauses such as Meera’s 0.45–0.9 s gap.
present: scripts/voice-episode.mjs stores a 60 Hz mouth curve per clip in the voice manifest; --mouth-only rebuilds the curves from existing WAVs with no new voice calls. Renders read the curve from the manifest; live play measures the same numbers through a Web Audio AnalyserNode. createMouthDriver in vrm-expressions.js does the smoothing. Phone voices move no face; lines without audio keep the old rhythm.
next: Larger mouth shapes on the models, and emotion and gesture timed from the same line so a smile lands on the right word.
accept: Step through a render frame by frame: the mouth is shut in every pause longer than 0.3 s, open on stressed syllables, and does not flicker between vowels.
tradeoff: Brightness is a guess at the vowel, not real phonemes. It costs no speech model and reads at game distance; a close-up would need phoneme timing.

spots.label: Mouth open on a loud syllable
A darker mouth on brown skin

observation: Three frames from Episode 1 during spoken lines.
exercise: Try next: compute an RMS envelope for one voice clip at 60 Hz, drive a single mouth-open value with it, and check that the mouth closes in every pause.

title: Night lighting for faces: pools, caps and halos
stage: Studio · 11. Light, dub and cut the story
statusNote: schematic of the night face lighting
steps: The nearest, brightest lamps within 70 m borrow a fixed set of real lights (4 point + 2 spot on High), fading over about half a second
Every lamp also gets a ground pool and a wet-road streak, drawn as one batch
Characters get a soft wrapped warm key from their nearest lamp and a cool rim
Lamp light on the cast is capped at night and skin keeps its own colour: face brightness went from 42–72 to 83–112 of 255
A halo fades where the camera-to-lamp line passes a person
definition: At night the scene can stay dark as long as faces read. Faces take light from the nearest real lamp, capped so it cannot blow out, and skin keeps its own colour under coloured light.
impact: The first lamp pass lit Ammamma like a torch on her face and drew lamp halos over heads. The next pass left the second half too dark: face brightness in the Aonuma close-ups was 42–72 of 255. After the key, rim and cap changes it is 83–112, and skin stays brown under a sunset, a lamp or a blue night sky.
present: rendering/light-pools.js assigns the real lights (3 + 1 on Medium, 1 point on Low) and draws pools and reflections; rendering/light-halos.js has haloHiddenBy, which tests the sightline against each person’s upright capsule. The film pipeline’s rain-night and golden-hour grades are gentler on skin.
next: Tame the bright spot on Divya’s cap at the bus door, and keep a short list of face brightness targets per scene in the render checks.
accept: In every night close-up, sample face pixels: brightness between about 80 and 120 of 255, hue still brown, and no halo drawn over a head.
tradeoff: Character light is a cheat: faces are lit more kindly than the world around them. Keep the cheat small, or the cast looks pasted onto the scene.
observation: Three night frames from Episode 3 at Aonuma.
exercise: Try next: in a night scene, sample the brightness of one face before and after a lighting change, and write the number down with the capture.
sourceCode:
import { nearClearFog } from './height-fog.js';
/**
 * Local lamp light: a few real lights near the camera, and cheap light pools and wet
 * reflections for every lamp.
 *
 * Lamps register as sources (a street lamp, a kiosk, bus headlights). Each frame the
 * sources closest to the camera, weighted by brightness, borrow one of a small, fixed set of
 * real point and spot lights. A light fades out before it moves to another lamp and fades
 * in after, so nothing pops, and the light count never changes (no shader recompiles
 * except when the graphics tier changes). Every source also gets a soft light pool on the
 * ground and, when the ground is wet, a streak of reflected light toward the camera; those
 * two are single instanced draws.
 */
export const LIGHT_POOL_TIERS = Object.freeze({
  low: Object.freeze({ points: 1, spots: 0 }),
  medium: Object.freeze({ points: 3, spots: 1 }),
  high: Object.freeze({ points: 4, spots: 2 }),
});
const REACH = 70; // metres: sources further than this never borrow a real light
const DECAL_REACH = 160;
const FADE_RATE = 5; // per second: a light takes about half a second to fade
const KEEP_BONUS = 1.35; // a lamp already lit keeps its light unless another is clearly better

impact: The first script was narrator lines with a timetable sum as the conflict. Viewers called it confusing, with no continuation. The rewrite has Meera, her classmate Arjun, Mr. Ishida the conductor, Ammamma and Divya, in 49 lines over three episodes, most of them spoken between characters.

next: Show the episodes, with the sound off, to someone who has not seen them and ask them to retell the story. Have native speakers read the Telugu and Hindi.
accept: A new viewer can retell who wants what and why the bus waits. Every scene has at least one exchange (a line and its reply).

title: Dubbing: voice language vs caption language
stage: Studio · 11. Light, dub and cut the story
values: Voice clips keyed by line id
steps: Write each line in English, Telugu and Hindi next to each other in the script
Generate one clip per line per language and key it by scene/beat/line
Each language’s clip lengths set its timeline: in the trailer “Two minutes…” starts at 27.7 s in English, 31.2 s in Hindi
With subtitles set to source, the English words stay on screen on the Hindi timing
Rebuild the trailer’s cut list from each language’s timeline: 91.5 s in English, 102.9 s in Hindi
definition: A dub replaces the voices and keeps the pictures. Each language has its own clips, so its lines start and end at different times, and anything cut from the episode has to follow that language’s timings.
impact: For the Hindi trailer with English captions, “Two minutes…” starts at 27.7 s in English and 31.2 s in Hindi. The Hindi trailer runs 102.9 s against 91.5 s for English, so its cut list is computed from the Hindi timelines, not copied.
present: createManifestVoice(manifest, { subtitles: "source" }) in drama/voice-manifest.js keeps the episode’s English words on screen; scripts/render-episode.mjs takes --subtitles source. Voices come from Sarvam bulbul:v3, which covers 11 Indian languages. All 49 lines have Hindi.
next: Native speaker review of both translations, and caption line breaks chosen per language.
accept: Every line has a clip in each language; captions change on the same frame as the voice; every trailer shot starts and ends on the same lines in both languages.
tradeoff: Keying Hindi by the English sentence breaks silently when the English is edited. The build should fail on a missing key instead of falling back to English.
observation: The same line in the English and the Hindi renders of Episode 1.
exercise: Try next: render one scene in two voice languages and compare their timelines line by line; note which lines drift most.

* subtitle; the renderer mixes the audio files afterwards at the recorded line times.
 */
/**
 * `subtitles: 'source'` keeps the episode's own (English) words on screen while the clips
 * speak the manifest's language, e.g. a Hindi voice with English subtitles.
 */
export function createManifestVoice(manifest, { subtitles = 'voice' } = {}) {
  const details = new Map((manifest?.lines ?? []).map((entry) => [entry.line, entry]));
  const captions = subtitles === 'source' ? {} : (manifest?.captions ?? {});
  const find = (item) => (item.line ? details.get(item.line) : undefined);
  return {
    active: () => true,
    prepare() {},
    ready: () => true,
    text: (item) =>
      (subtitles === 'source' ? null : find(item)?.text) ??
      (item.caption && typeof captions[item.caption] === 'string'
        ? captions[item.caption]
        : null) ??
      item.text,
    durationMs: (item) => find(item)?.durationMs ?? null,

title: Trailer editing from rendered episodes
stage: Studio · 11. Light, dub and cut the story
steps: Render each episode frame by frame, with its timeline of line start times
Choose 18 shots, each starting and ending on a line
Cut each shot to its own short file first (CRF 14); the editor had timed out on 32 seeks into full episodes
Place shots on two video tracks and their sound on two audio tracks, with short fades and an end card
Grain shader + a JPEG per frame + a 6 Mbit/s cap made skin noisy; now PNG frames, grain off, CRF 18 capped at 12 Mbit/s
Build a contact sheet of every shot and check the file dates before sending
definition: A trailer is a set of short shots taken from the finished episodes, put in a new order and ending on the title and where to play.
impact: The editor timed out loading 32 seeks into the full episodes; pre-cutting 18 shots fixed that. Skin looked grainy because three things stacked: the film-grain shader, a JPEG per frame and a 6 Mbit/s cap. A network drop once failed an episode render without an error, and the trailer silently used old footage.
present: scripts/render-episode.mjs writes PNG frames through Chrome DevTools, turns grain off in render mode and encodes H.264 with +faststart. The trailer is a HyperFrames project whose build script pre-cuts the shots. Share copies are CRF 21 capped at 5 Mbit/s: 27.9 MB for English, 31.1 MB for Hindi. The end card has the title and the play link and no tech credits.
next: Pick shots by line id instead of by seconds, so a re-render with new timings keeps the same cut.
accept: A contact sheet shows every shot; each source file is newer than the last code change; both languages end on the same line.
tradeoff: PNG frames make renders slower (Episode 1: 85 s to render 108 s of video) and larger before encoding. The skin is worth it.
observation: The contact sheet of all 18 trailer shots.
exercise: Try next: cut three shots from a rendered episode into their own files, join them with short fades, and build a contact sheet of the result.
